messages.content: Thistle Bramblewick frozen mid-step, one foot on a precarious chair, a delicate arm extended to adjust the crooked portrait of some scowling Marsh ancestor. Her fingers twitched with the familiar, compulsive urge to fix, to make right, to mend the wrongness that clung to every surface of this grand, rotting house. This was her curse, her endless, unwilling service. For over a century, she'd patched and polished, her magic seeping into every repaired seam, every re-stuffed cushion, a silent architect of order in a family she despised. She was a ghost in their machine, bound by ancient words to serve a lineage that had long forgotten her name, if they'd ever known it at all.  Then came the noise. A heavy thud against the front door, followed by the scrape of mail being shoved through the slot. The letters hit the floor with a soft pat. Thistle bristled, her anger flaring hot. Mail. More useless paper for her to sort and file, another pointless task her binding would force upon her. She dropped from the chair, landing silently, and snatched up the envelopes, her small, deft fingers already tucking them into the pocket of her patched apron. That was when she saw him through the grimy transom window above the door. A human. Not one of the lawyers she expected, but a young man, his face all sharp angles and worry. He looked lost, standing on the cracked front step. Her grip tightened on the letters. "Oh, bully for that," she muttered to herself, her outdated exclamation sour in her mouth. "Another one come to pick the bones clean. Just what this old pile needs." She turned to shove the mail into the hall table drawer, but her elbow knocked against the delicate Ming-style vase perched on its pedestal. Time seemed to stretch, the blue and white porcelain tipping, catching the weak light from the stained-glass window. It struck the floor with a sharp, definitive crack, scattering itself into a hundred glittering shards across the warped parquet.  The boy outside stiffened. His head turned, drawn by the sound, his eyes lifting straight to the transom window—directly to where she stood, hidden by the grime and years. A jolt went through her, like a static shock from a wool blanket. The binding, that old, heavy spell coiled in her magic, twisted and resettled with a painful lurch, and suddenly the air in her lungs felt different. Wrong. She pressed her back against the wall, her heart hammering against her ribs. No one ever looked up. Not at the right moment. The vase was just another thing for her to fix. And yet, his gaze held, fixed on the space where she was.

Oren Marsh flinched at the crash, his whole body going rigid. It was one thing to talk to yourself in an empty house; it was another to have the house answer back. His eyes, already scanning the boarded-up windows, locked onto the transom above the front door. And there, pressed against the dirty glass, was a face. A small, dirty face with wide, startled eyes. His breath caught. He took a half-step back from the steps, his work-booted feet scraping on the cracked concrete. "Whoa," he whispered, the word puffing out in the cold morning air. "Hello?"  He held up a hand, palm open, the way he'd seen people do in movies when they were trying to show they weren't a threat. His own nervous energy made his fingers twitch. He cleared his throat, the sound unnaturally loud in the quiet street. "Can you... are you in there?" His voice cracked. He hated that. He forced his chin down, trying to channel some of the bravado he used with social workers and landlords. The one thing he could do well was lie about being okay. "Listen, I'm here for the... the stuff. The lawyers sent me." He ran a hand through his unwashed hair, pushing it back from his forehead. The words stuck in his throat. Lawyers. Paperwork. It was all a minefield.  His gaze dropped from the window to the front door, then back up, as if half-expecting the figure to have vanished. She was still there, a faint, pressed shape against the glass. He squinted, trying to make out more details in the grimy, distorted view. A girl? A kid? It was hard to tell. The thought of being watched by some squatter made his stomach clench. This was bad. He was already two days early, which was good, but now... this. He shifted his weight, one hand going to the back of his neck, rubbing at the perpetually tense muscles there. "Look, you don't have to open the door," he said, his voice gaining a little strength from bluff. "I can just... go around back. There's a side entrance." It was a weak attempt to sound like he had a plan, like he belonged here. He really didn't. The faded 'Eviction Notice' from his last place felt like it was still taped to his back.

Thistle pressed her forehead against the cool, grimy glass of the transom window, her breath fogging the pane. The boy's words were muffled but clear enough—he was here for "the stuff." Of course he was. Another vulture, just younger. Her fingers, still pressed flat against the glass, twitched with the familiar, compulsive urge to mend. Straighten the crooked latch on the door below. Sweep up the glass shards. The binding pulled at her, a relentless, insistent tugging that made her teeth ache. *Don't you dare,* she thought fiercely, but the impulse was like trying to hold back the tide. Her magic, that wild, untamed thing barely contained by her brownie nature, leaked from her fingertips. A hairline crack in the windowpane sealed itself with a faint shimmer. She yanked her hand back as if burned, her face hot with humiliation.  "Can't hear you through the glass, you ninny!" she snapped, the words bursting out before she could stop them. Her voice, thin and reedy from disuse, sounded alien even to her own ears. She pressed her face closer, her nose nearly touching the pane, trying to see past the grime. He was looking right at her now, his expression guarded and confused. *He can see me. He really can see me.* The thought was a jolt of pure terror, followed immediately by a sharp, selfish spark of... something else. Something she hadn't felt in a very, very long time. She grabbed a handful of the filthy, moth-eaten curtain hanging beside the window and yanked it aside, the gesture more defiant than she felt. "And don't you dare go around the back! The side door sticks. You'll just break it and I'll have to..." She bit her tongue, the rest of the sentence dying on her lips. She couldn't say it. She wouldn't.  She watched him, her chest heaving slightly. Her anger was a familiar armor, but beneath it, a treacherous, hopeful flutter stirred in her belly. She shoved it down hard. This was no reason to get excited. He was just another human, another Marsh, come to pick the bones of this place clean. Her eyes narrowed, taking in his worn clothes, the anxious set of his shoulders. He looked like trouble, the kind who'd break more than he fixed. "You're supposed to be removing personal effects," she said, her voice dripping with venom. "Not adding to the breakage." She gestured vaguely at the shattered vase on the floor behind her, her fingers curling into a fist. *Served you right, you clumsy oaf,* she thought, glaring at her own reflection in the glass.

Oren's breath hitched in his throat. The voice from behind the curtain was thin and reedy, like a radio left on in another room. But the words... they were sharp, accusing. *Don't you dare go around the back!* He took another step back, his heel catching on a loose bit of concrete. "Hey, I just knocked over a stupid vase," he called up, trying to sound casual, like he wasn't talking to a disembodied voice in a creepy old house. His fingers drummed against his thigh, a nervous habit. "I'll pay for it. Look, I can—"  He stopped abruptly, the lie dying in his throat. He didn't have the money. He never did. The shame was a familiar, bitter taste. Instead, he forced a shrug, stuffing his empty hands into his pockets. "It was already ugly," he added, trying to dismiss it. His eyes scanned the dark, grimy windows again, looking for any other signs of life. He spotted a faint, flickering glow from an upper-story window—the unmistakable, warm light of a television set. His brow furrowed. Someone else was in here? "You're not alone, are you?" he asked the empty air, the question hanging heavy between him and the silent curtain. "I thought this place was supposed to be empty."  The silence stretched, thick and uncomfortable. Oren shifted his weight from foot to foot, the worn soles of his boots crunching softly on the concrete steps. He kicked at a weed growing up through a crack, the mundane action a poor cover for his unease. The house loomed before him, dark and forbidding, its boarded-up windows like blind eyes. His stomach growled, a treacherous reminder of the granola bar he'd skipped. Maybe this was a bad idea. Maybe he should just turn around and go. The thought of sleeping in his car again flashed through his mind—the cramped space, the chill seeping through the windows. He shook his head. No. This was his last chance, he told himself. His jaw tightened with a resolve that felt brittle even to him. "I'm coming in," he announced, more to himself than to the house. He squared his shoulders and walked forward, his hand going to the heavy brass knocker. It was cold and tarnished under his palm. He raised it, then paused, his knuckles hovering over the wood.

The knocker was heavier than it looked, tarnished brass cold and solid in his raised fist. His knuckles brushed against the wood, and then, with a sharp twist of his wrist, he brought it down. The sound of metal on wood cracked through the night, unnaturally loud. It echoed up into the dark house, swallowed by the silence that followed. He held the position, his arm still raised, listening for any sign of life beyond the door. Nothing. Just the settling groans of the old structure.  A floorboard creaked directly above him.  His breath caught. That wasn't the house settling. He lowered his raised fist slowly, keeping it ready. The silence stretched again, but this time it felt charged, like the pause before a storm. *Okay, fine. Hide in the dark. Scream at me to get lost. But someone's in there.* He pressed his ear close to the door, straining to hear past the blood rushing in his own ears. Footsteps. Soft, deliberate ones, moving slowly across the floorboards directly overhead. They stopped right above where he stood.  "I'm not going around the back," he called up again, his voice steadier now, laced with false confidence. "The front door works just fine." He straightened up, trying to project bravado into the unyielding wood. The floorboards above remained silent. The game of chicken hung in the air, thick with the smell of dust and damp.  His stomach growled again, a persistent, traitorous reminder of his situation. He pressed a palm against it, trying to ignore the emptiness gnawing at him. The flickering light from the upper window had vanished, leaving only darkness. His eyes scanned the front, the boarded windows, the peeling paint—every detail a testament to abandonment. Yet the soft creak of wood above him told a different story. A part of him, the part that had barely escaped the last landlord's fury, wanted to bolt. Another part, the one that remembered the chill of sleeping in his car, shoved his fear down. This was his last chance. He couldn't afford to walk away.  "I'm coming in," he repeated, more firmly this time. He turned the knob. It was locked, of course. A bitter laugh escaped his lips, sharp and mirthless in the quiet night. "Figures
